In 2009, his re-election was supported only by the [[Democratic Liberal Party (Romania)|Democratic Liberal Party]] (PDL) along with a certain faction of the [[Christian Democratic National Peasants' Party]] (PNȚCD);}} | rowspan="2" | {{cite web|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/1056376.html|title=Romania: Basescu Wins Presidential Vote, Vows To Fight Corruption|work=Radio Free Europe|author=Eugen Tomiuc|date=13 December 2004|accessdate=5 April 2022}} |- | colspan="4" style="font-size:85%;" | Elected with the support of the right-leaning [[Justice and Truth Alliance]] (DA), Băsescu won the presidency in [[2004 Romanian general election|2004]] on a platform targeting widespread [[political corruption]]. During his first term, Romania [[2007 enlargement of the European Union|joined in the European Union]] (EU). In spite of the harsh opposition of the [[left-wing politics|left-leaning]] parties (especially the PSD and the [[Greater Romania Party|PRM]]), he publicly [[Presidential Commission for the Study of the Communist Dictatorship in Romania|condemned the former communist regime]]. His second term was marked by a [[landslide victory]] of the opposition coalition, specifically the [[Social Liberal Union]] (USL), in both the [[2012 Romanian local elections|local]] and the [[2012 Romanian parliamentary election|legislative elections]] of 2012, amidst heavy losses for the presidential party (i.e. the Democratic Liberal Party). Internationally, Băsescu aligned Romania closer to the [[United States]], the [[European Union]] (EU), and [[NATO]], maintaining a pro-[[Western world|Western]] foreign policy throughout both his terms. He was suspended twice, namely in [[2007 Romanian presidential impeachment referendum|2007]] and [[2012 Romanian presidential impeachment referendum|2012]]. Both impeachment referendums were invalidated by the [[Constitutional Court of Romania|Constitutional Court]] on the grounds of low turnout, thus paving his way for a comeback to presidency. |- style="background-color: #eee;" ! rowspan=2 style="background:{{party color|National Liberal Party (Romania)}}; color:black" | 5 |rowspan=2|[[File:Клаус Йоханнис (52539721210).jpg|80px]] |rowspan=2|'''[[Klaus Iohannis]]'''

[[2019 Romanian presidential election|2019]] | 21 December 2014 | 12 February 2025 |{{age in years and days|2014|12|21|2025|02|12}} |[[National Liberal Party (Romania)|National Liberal Party]] (PNL) |rowspan=3|{{cite news|work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2014/nov/16/romania-klaus-iohannis-president |title=Klaus Iohannis wins Romanian presidential election |date=November 16, 2014 |access-date=November 17, 2014 |archive-date=November 17, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141117064758/http://www.theguardian.com/world/2014/nov/16/romania-klaus-iohannis-president |url-status=live }} |- | colspan="4" style="font-size:85%;"|Elected with the support of the right-leaning [[Christian Liberal Alliance]] (ACL), Iohannis won against former USL ally and coalition partner [[Victor Ponta]] in the run-off of the 2014 Romanian presidential elections. During the presidential campaign, his platform focused on [[anti-corruption]], [[judicial independence]], and [[Fiscal policy|fiscal relaxation]].{{cite web|url=https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/presidents-of-romania-since-1989.html|title=Presidents of Romania since 1989|work=World Atlas|accessdate=1 July 2018}} He is also the first Romanian President to have stemmed from an [[minorities of Romania|ethnic minority]], as he is of [[Germans of Romania|German]] (more specifically [[Transylvanian Saxons|Transylvanian Saxon]]) origin.{{cite web|url=https://euobserver.com/political/126530|title=Romanians elect first ethnic German president|work=EU Observer|date=17 November 2014| accessdate= 19 June 2018}} In the wake of the [[2016 Romanian legislative election|2016 legislative elections]], his first presidential term was marked by the frequent change of prime ministers made by his former and current close allies, the social democrats, as well as by the [[2017–2019 Romanian protests|most massive and widespread series of protests]] to have ever occurred in the history of Romania (which were directed against the political corruption supposedly endorsed by the social democratic governments). After defeating PSD candidate [[Viorica Dăncilă]] by a landslide in both presidential election rounds during late 2019, his second term has been marked by the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Romania|COVID-19 pandemic]] and by further political instability (resulting in the [[2021 Romanian political crisis]]) and [[democratic backsliding]]. In 2023, Iohannis faced a [[2023 Romanian teachers' strike|general strike of the Romanian teachers]]. His second term was also subject to multiple political errors and controversies. |- ! colspan=3 |— | style="background-color: #eee;" |''[[2024 Romanian presidential election|2024]]'' | colspan="4" style="font-size:85%;"|The [[Constitutional Court of Romania]] annulled the 2024 presidential election after [[far-right]] candidate [[Călin Georgescu]] took a shock lead in the first round, over allegations of Russian covert interference and illegal campaign spending by Georgescu. Dan ran on a strongly [[pro-Western]], [[anti-corruption]] platform, contrasting sharply with the [[Romanian nationalism|nationalist]] and [[Eurosceptic]] stance of the election's then front-runner, [[George Simion]].
